title: Medicare and working past age 65
summary: Guide to Medicare decisions for people who keep working past 65, including employer size rules, delaying Part A and B, creditable drug coverage, COBRA, TRICARE, FEHB and the retirement Special Enrollment Period.

assets.alt: Your Medicare Special Enrollment Period calendar
Working past 65: When you may be able to delay Medicare

atoms.title: Getting ready if you plan to work past 65
atoms.question: I plan to work past age 65. What do I need to do about Medicare?
atoms.text: Start researching your Medicare options at least 6 months before your 65th birthday, looking for coverage that meets your needs. Find out the dates for your Initial Enrollment Period (IEP), a 7-month period surrounding your 65th birthday. You may not need to enroll in both Part A and Part B right away, but knowing your IEP dates will help you plan.

atoms.title: Employer size and your Medicare options
atoms.question: Do I have to get Medicare if I have employer coverage?
atoms.text: If you are still working and have health coverage through your employer or union, including federal or state employment, active-duty military service, or a spouse's work, you may want to delay Medicare. If your employer has fewer than 20 employees, you may need to enroll in Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period. If your employer has 20 or more employees, you may delay Medicare enrollment, drop your employer coverage for Medicare, or have both. For a spouse's employer, review the employer's rules.

atoms.title: Questions for your benefits administrator
atoms.question: What should I ask my benefits administrator before enrolling in Medicare?
atoms.text: The main question to ask your benefits administrator is whether you should keep your existing coverage. Ask if Medicare can work with your employer plan and if retiree coverage is available. Also ask how changing your insurance would affect your spouse and any dependents, and find out whether they will be eligible for COBRA if you drop employer coverage.

atoms.title: Delaying both Part A and Part B
atoms.question: Can I delay Medicare Part A and Part B without penalty?
atoms.text: If you qualify, you can delay both Medicare Part A and Part B without penalty. When you stop working or lose employer coverage, whichever comes first, you will need to enroll during a Special Enrollment Period. To avoid Part D penalties, you will also need to provide written proof of creditable prescription drug coverage, meaning a plan expected to pay, on average, at least as much as Medicare drug coverage does.

atoms.title: Enrolling in Part A only while working
atoms.question: Can I enroll in only Part A while I'm still working?
atoms.text: Medicare Part A is premium-free for most people, so you could enroll in only Part A while still working. If you have a health savings account (HSA), you will have to stop making contributions once you enroll in Part A. You can still use the funds for qualified medical expenses, including some Medicare costs such as premiums, deductibles and copays.

atoms.title: Why some people delay Part B
atoms.question: Why would someone delay enrolling in Part B while working?
atoms.text: Medicare Part B charges a premium. Some people who work past 65 and have employer coverage delay enrolling in Part B and postpone paying the premium, then sign up later during a Special Enrollment Period. In some situations, such as when an employer has fewer than 20 employees, you may need to get Part B during your Initial Enrollment Period to avoid penalties. Most people pay the standard Part B premium, and people with higher incomes may pay more.

atoms.title: Check for creditable drug coverage before delaying
atoms.question: Why do I need creditable drug coverage before delaying Medicare?
atoms.text: Before you officially delay Medicare, make sure you have creditable drug coverage, meaning your employer provides drug coverage at least as good as standard Medicare Part D coverage. If your employer's drug coverage isn't creditable, you will need to enroll in a Part D plan during your Initial Enrollment Period to avoid the Part D late enrollment penalty. You will also need to get either Part A or Part B in order to get a Part D plan.

atoms.title: Having both Medicare and employer coverage
atoms.question: Can I have both Medicare and employer coverage?
atoms.text: Yes. Ask your benefits administrator how your employer plan will work with Medicare. Depending on your situation, one will act as your primary coverage and one as secondary.

atoms.title: How COBRA and Medicare work together
atoms.question: How do COBRA and Medicare work together?
atoms.text: If you have COBRA before Medicare, you will need to enroll in Medicare when you become eligible; you may delay Part D if COBRA includes creditable drug coverage, otherwise you have 63 days to get Part D without penalty after losing COBRA. If you enroll in Medicare Part A and Part B before COBRA, you can have both, but COBRA is optional, Medicare is primary and COBRA is secondary. If you enroll in Part A only before COBRA, you must enroll in Part B within eight months of your employment ending to avoid penalties.

atoms.title: TRICARE, CHAMPVA and FEHB with Medicare
atoms.question: How do TRICARE, CHAMPVA and FEHB work with Medicare?
atoms.text: If you have TRICARE or CHAMPVA coverage, you will need to see if you qualify for premium-free Part A; if eligible, you may be required to enroll in both Part A and Part B to keep that coverage, and if not eligible, enrollment is optional but late penalties are possible. If you receive Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB), you can delay enrolling in Part A and/or Part B if your insurance is based on employment, or a spouse's employment, with an employer that has 20 or more employees.

atoms.title: Enrolling in Medicare when you retire
atoms.question: What happens when I retire if I delayed Medicare?
atoms.text: If you qualify for Medicare and delay enrollment past age 65, you will have a Special Enrollment Period once you retire or lose your employer coverage. If you choose a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage or a standalone Part D plan, you have 63 days to enroll without penalty. If you choose Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) only, you have up to 8 months. The 8-month SEP gives up to 8 months for Parts A and/or B, but only the first two months to enroll in Parts C and/or D.

atoms.title: Notify Social Security to delay Part B
atoms.question: What else do I need to do if I delay Medicare enrollment?
atoms.text: If you receive Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, you should be enrolled in Medicare Part A and Part B automatically when you turn 65. If you receive Social Security benefits and are eligible for Medicare, you should enroll in Part A. If you want to delay enrollment in Part B, you will need to notify the Social Security Administration.
